extracted.intended_audience: practical geometers / land surveyors and students of geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural geometric rules and constructions for measuring triangles and areas in practice (land surveying), using equidistant lines, similarity/proportions, perpendiculars, scaled similar figures and arithmetic manipulations to eliminate radicals. Includes worked numeric examples and practical measurement advice (ropes, stakes, counting units).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use lines equidistant to a side to create similar triangles
rubrics_metrics.description: Draw a line equidistant to a given side of a triangle; the figures so obtained are similar to portions of the original and yield proportional relations between segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text repeatedly instructs drawing a line equidistant to side a g (e.g. 'equediftante ala linea a g') and using the resulting similar triangles to derive proportionalities among corresponding segments and to transfer measurements from one triangle to another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similar triangles imply proportional sides and proportional areas (squares of sides)
rubrics_metrics.description: Triangles that are similar (equal angles or constructed by equidistant/parallel lines) have proportional corresponding sides; their areas are proportional to the squares of corresponding sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used throughout: when triangles are 'fimili' or 'simili', one may set up ratios of sides (e.g. b:g :: a:c) and deduce area relations by comparing squares ('il quadrato od la linea...'). Examples and arithmetic manipulations show multiplying squares to compute areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area of a triangle from base and altitude (catetto)
rubrics_metrics.description: The area of a triangle is obtained by the product of a base and its corresponding altitude (catetto), with appropriate halving according to the usual base*height/2 relation expressed via construction and multiplication of segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedures instruct multiplying a catetto by the corresponding 'lamita' and then taking necessary divisions; practical measurement instructions convert these geometric products into countable units. Several worked examples multiply catheti and sides to obtain the triangle's area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure by constructing a much larger similar triangle and counting units
rubrics_metrics.description: To measure an irregular field, construct on the ground a much larger triangle similar to the theoretical one so that the measured units (e.g., rows, 'biade') inside it can be counted; then scale down by the known proportional factor to get the actual area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text advises making the triangle as large as needed 'affinche il catetto... non si poteffe'][sic]' and counting how many small units fall along sides/areas. It gives practical notes (ropes, stakes) and numeric scaling examples showing how to multiply/divide counts to recover the true area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide segments into proportional parts to determine unknown sides
rubrics_metrics.description: When some side lengths are unknown, divide known lines into equal parts and use proportionality of similar triangles (constructed via equidistant lines or parallels) to infer the unknown segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many constructions split lines at points (e.g., dividing segment into two equal parts at D) and use the proportionality relations (e.g., 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 factors) to express unknown sides as multiples of known units; the text gives iterative examples of dividing and multiplying segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use perpendiculars from given points to establish catheti and right-triangle relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Drop perpendiculars (construct right angles) from given points to sides to create right triangles where catheti (altitudes) can be measured or used in proportional constructions for area/sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructions such as 'menando vna perpendiculare al bg' and procedures for locating the foot of a perpendicular (point where a cathetus falls) are given; these perpendiculars are then used as 'catetto' in multiplication to obtain areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: When only one side (or a point on a side) is known, construct equidistant/parallel lines to determine other sides and the area
rubrics_metrics.description: If a single side and/or a point on a side is known, create lines equidistant to that side and use intersections and similar-triangle arguments to compute the remaining sides and area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives multi-step recipes: choose a point, draw an equidistant line, trace parallels/perpendiculars to obtain similar triangles, divide segments into proportional parts and multiply to get area. Numerous stepwise examples appear (points A, B, D, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear irrationalities by multiplying lengths by convenient integers so squared lengths become integral
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid roots/radicals in computation, multiply the given lengths by an appropriately chosen integer (e.g., 720, 28800 in examples) so that the squares (quadrati) of those lengths become whole numbers and arithmetic can proceed by ordinary multiplication/division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise explicitly demonstrates picking multipliers (examples: 720, 28800, 820, 100, etc.) so that resulting squared quantities are integer multiples; then perform algebraic manipulations on those integers and at the end divide by the chosen factors to recover the true geometric measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent lengths with their squares (quadrati) when computing areas and proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the square of a line (quadrato della linea) as the algebraic object in computations involving areas and proportional relations, since areas correspond naturally to squared units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manuscript repeatedly forms 'il quadrato od la linea' and adds/multiplies such squares to get area-related quantities; examples show how adding squares of certain segments and multiplying by factors yields the area or comparative measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit equal angles (equiangoli) to assert similarity and transfer measures
rubrics_metrics.description: When triangles share equal angles (are equiangoli), they are similar and one may transfer proportional relations of sides and derived areas between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several lemmas note 'triangoli ... sono equiangoli' and then use that to equate ratios of sides and deduce area ratios, often via constructing auxiliary lines that produce equal angles and hence similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use midpoint and point-division constructions to find 'cadimento' (foot) of catheti for measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide a segment into two equal parts at a point (the midpoint) or otherwise locate the foot where a cathetus (altitude) falls by iterative placements of ropes/filaments to find the exact position to measure heights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical instructions: use a thread/rope placed so it just touches a given face to locate where a cathetus falls; divide that segment into two equal parts at the touching point; the part indicates the altitude and is used in subsequent multiplications for area. The manuscript describes moving the thread and dividing the resulting touch points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical measuring: use ropes/threads and countable small measures for accurate field measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: On the ground, use ropes, threads and small measured units (a small sample length or 'mifurato piccio' and counting 'biade' or planted rows) to convert geometric constructions into countable quantities for arithmetic scaling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explicitly recommends constructing a large triangle with ropes and counting how many 'biade' (units) fall along lines; then use the numeric proportional relations to scale the counted units to the true area. This is the recommended practical surveying method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use arithmetic proportional operations (multiply/divide) consistent with geometric similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow proportional arithmetic rules: multiply corresponding segments, divide by chosen partitions, and combine ratios consistent with the similarity relations to compute unknown lengths and areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many worked examples show sequences of multiplications/divisions (e.g., multiply by 2, divide by 4, multiply by selected integers) to carry through the construction computations; also guidance about permuting proportional factors and using integer scaling to keep computations integral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partition an area or side into known fractional parts and use recombination to compute area
rubrics_metrics.description: If a line or area can be partitioned into known fractional parts (1/2, 1/4, 1/8, etc.), use those fractional pieces and recombine (add/multiply) to obtain the overall area or to reconstruct unknown lengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manuscript demonstrates successive halving and addition of parts (e.g., divide in two, then in four) and recombining via multiplication to produce target ratios; used when exact proportional partitions are obtainable practically on the field.
